paragraphs.heading: What it means
paragraphs.text: A half-life, written t_½, is the time it takes for an amount of something to drop to half of what it started at. The word is common in nuclear physics, where it describes how fast unstable atoms decay. It is also used for any exponential decay, and occasionally for decay that is not exponential. Medicine, for instance, talks about the biological half-life of drugs and other chemicals inside the human body.

paragraphs.heading: A steady clock
paragraphs.text: For a quantity that shrinks exponentially, the half-life stays the same the whole time. Its mirror image is doubling time, which measures growth by a factor of 2 instead of shrinking by it. Ernest Rutherford discovered the principle in 1907 and called it the half-life period, a name cut down to half-life in the early 1950s. He used it to work out the ages of rocks, by measuring the decay of radium to lead-206.

paragraphs.heading: A matter of chance
paragraphs.text: Radioactive atoms come as separate units, which causes a problem. If you have one atom with a half-life of one second, you will not find half an atom after a second. So the half-life is defined by probability: it is the time in which exactly half the atoms decay on average. Put another way, each atom has a 50% chance of decaying within one half-life. With many identical atoms, the law of large numbers makes half remaining a very good approximation, and flipping coins can act this out.

paragraphs.heading: The decay constant
paragraphs.text: The half-life is tied to a second number, the decay constant λ, which is always positive. The link is t_(1/2) = (ln (2))/λ, where ln(2), the natural logarithm of 2, is about 0.693. For radioactive atoms, the half-life depends on the type of atom and isotope. It is usually found by experiment.

paragraphs.heading: In chemical reactions
paragraphs.text: In chemistry, the half-life of a substance is the time for its concentration to fall to half its starting value. In a first order reaction, the rate is proportional to how much reactant there is, so the concentration falls exponentially. Its half-life, t_(1/2) = (ln 2)/k, depends only on the rate constant k and not on the starting concentration. In a zero order reaction, the rate does not depend on concentration, which falls in a straight line, and the half-life does depend on the starting concentration.

paragraphs.heading: In the body and beyond
paragraphs.text: A biological half-life is the time a substance, such as a drug or a radioactive nuclide, takes to lose half of its pharmacologic, physiologic or radiological activity. Clearing a substance from a living body usually follows more complex kinetics than radioactive decay does. The biological half-life of water in a person is about 9 to 10 days, though behavior and other conditions can change it, and for caesium it is one to four months. Epidemiologists use the idea too, for the time it takes the number of new cases in an outbreak to halve.
